analysis.one_liner: Shields the first $1,000 of a worker's weekly pay from garnishment by creditors.
analysis.headline: The bill would have shielded the first $1,000 a worker earns each week from garnishment, but it never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed federal law so that creditors could not garnish the first $1,000 of a worker's weekly take-home pay, with that amount rising each year with inflation. It also would have explicitly banned employers from firing or penalizing workers whose wages get garnished, and barred debt collectors from trying to have debtors arrested or jailed. It never moved past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage and essential workers whose wages face garnishment for debts: they would keep the first $1,000 of weekly take-home pay untouched, a floor that rises with inflation. Workers currently can lose up to a quarter of their disposable earnings to garnishment; this would protect the pay needed for rent and groceries. It would also protect any worker from being fired or disciplined because of a garnishment, and shield debtors from collection tactics aimed at getting them arrested.

how_it_helps.text: It raises the floor on garnishment: under current law, creditors can take the lesser of 25% of disposable pay or the amount above a much lower (30-times-the-minimum-wage) exemption; the bill lets a worker keep the first $1,000 of weekly pay before any of the 25% calculation applies.
The $1,000 exemption rises each year with inflation (the Consumer Price Index), so the protection does not shrink in real terms over time.

It bars employers from firing or taking any adverse action against an employee because their wages were garnished, and strengthens the requirement that state laws provide at least equivalent protection.

It adds a new prohibition to the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act against debt collectors taking or threatening actions to have a debtor arrested or imprisoned, including seeking civil arrest warrants in state court.

analysis.who_pays: Creditors and debt collectors who would collect less from low-wage workers through garnishment, and potentially other consumers if lenders tighten credit to borrowers whose pay can no longer be garnished.

drawbacks.text: By shielding the first $1,000 per week from garnishment, the bill would make it harder for creditors — including lenders, landlords, and other judgment holders — to collect on legally owed debts, which could lead some lenders to restrict credit to low-income borrowers.
The bill does not reduce or forgive the underlying debt; it only slows collection, so creditors could pursue debtors through other means such as bank account levies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to low-wage workers with garnished paychecks is direct and meaningful, and the inflation indexing prevents the protection from eroding. The cost falls on creditors and debt collectors, who would recover less from low earners. A fair objection is that shielding wages entirely could make some lenders less willing to extend credit to low-income borrowers, tightening access to credit for the very people the bill helps; and protecting debtors does nothing about the underlying debts. Still, the bill got no committee action and no debate, so these tradeoffs were never weighed publicly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Alma Adams introduced the bill on October 25, 2022, in the final months of the 117th Congress.
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Creditors and debt collectors who garnish low-wage workers' paychecks are better off, because nothing now prevents them from continuing to garnish earnings above the old, much lower exemption.

for.name: Rep. Alma Adams (D-NC)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to shield the first $1,000 of weekly earnings from garnishment and bar debtor-imprisonment collection tactics.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no report — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill never advanced far enough for any vote, so no party split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill makes it harder to garnish low-wage workers' paychecks by protecting the first $1,000 of weekly earnings, and adds penalties for trying to have debtors arrested. Collections would slow or shrink for debts owed by low-income workers.

With less access to a borrower's paycheck, creditors would recover less from low-wage debtors and might tighten lending to them. The bill was referred to the Financial Services Committee, which has jurisdiction over this industry, but no action was taken.
